title: 2026 Bespoked Osaka: Cherubim All Road – Tamahagane – John Watson
content:
Cari and John are in Japan for the first 2026 Bespoked Osaka showcase. Before our show coverage kicks off, we’ve got Petor Georgallou‘s all-road bike he had built for the film project “Tamahagane, a story of Japanese steel” by legendary Japanese builders Cherubim. To celebrate Japanese design and craftsmanship, John photographed the bike in the courtyard of a Tadao Ando project entitled Osaka Culturarium at Tempozan…

Tamahagane

Japan is a country built on a history of craft and design. When Bespoked owner Petor Georgallou set out to create his film, “Tamahagane, a story of Japanese steel” he blended mythological lore with a visual history of steel in Japan. The film premiered at this year’s Bespoked Dresden and features an abstract vignette into the manufacturing of steel vis-à-vis the modern craft of framebuilding.

While the film shines a light primarily on the demands of Keirin racing on steel bikes, it also focuses on the work of legendary framebuilders Cherubim, following the Machida-based builders as they create this stunning all-road bike from tubing to final product.

Tamahagane, the film, shows the transition between mythology, industry, sport, culture and finally focuses on the making of their bike, which is built by Shinichi Konno – who is a traditional master NJS builder, but also the head of the Tokyo School of Bicycle Design working at the cutting edge of framebuilfing in Japan.

Cherubim All Road

Blending traditional lines and Keisei tubing diameters with a modern integrated headtube can present some challenges. Shinichi and his team abhor the look of 3D sintered, or printed, components on bicycles but acknowledged the technological edge they can give builders. Rather than printing lugs and simply polishing them smooth, the team of builders utilized the technology primarily to ensure the correct tolerances for the integrated bearings and head tube spec.

Cherubim then hand-carved the printed material into their desired form and shape, bringing the technology back into the truly handmade realm. The result is beautiful, chrome-plated lugs that mimic Cherubim’s legacy work while bringing the bike into the modern era with a wholly integrated cockpit and an Enve carbon all-road fork.

Its paint is inspired by the Cinelli Supercorsa, a nod to Japanese builders being inspired by Italian builders over the decades. Cherubim sourced the paint from Italy.

The brand continued this exercise in adopting modern standards with its own UDH dropout design to accommodate the Full Mount SRAM Red AXS XPLR derailleur. In the end, the project celebrates the craft and heritage of Japanese makers and the cycling industry, while also highlighting the Japanese builders’ readiness to create, collaborate, and work in a forward-thinking way with the most current and technologically advanced componentry on the market.

Sturdy Cycles CNC Titanium Stem

Much as Tadao Ando leaves his concrete raw, with the formwork texturing of wood present, along with the holes from the P-cones used in the cast-in-place concrete process, Tom Sturdy from Sturdy Cycles embraces the machine paths in his new CNC components. Tom made the switch from 3D printing to CNC a few years ago, and his new components are stunning.

Using the material to showcase the construction technique is both honest and stunning, creating a network of tightly woven machine paths. This visual language is something Tom will continue to evolve as his bike frames and components lean further into the art of computer numeric controlled design and fabrication.

Tadao Ando: Materialism

Much as Cherubim works with steel, a traditional Japanese manufacturing material, engineering the perfect ride quality for Keirin racers and customers alike, Japanese architect Tadao Ando uses concrete, a material popularized by the Béton brut movement of post WWII Europe, to design how light and tactility can enhance the visual and body-felt experience of buildings.

The Osaka Culturarium at Tempozan began as the Suntory Museum and sits waterfront on Osaka Bay. Completed in 1994 to commemorate Suntory’s 90th anniversary, this project was commissioned by Keizo Saji, a Japanese businessman and a lifelong fan of Ando’s work. At the time of commissioning the Suntory Museum, Saji was the second president of Suntory and was an influential art patron.

Pairing the work of Cherubim with an icon like Tadao Ando felt like a fitting way to kick off our Bespoked Osaka coverage. Showcasing untraditional means to an end is what framebuilder showcases are all about. This might have been a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to document two legacy artists together.
